terms.def: A subatomic particle found in the nucleus with relative mass 1 and relative charge +1.

terms.def: A subatomic particle found in the nucleus with relative mass 1 and relative charge 0.
terms.lessonName: Atomic structure — protons, neutrons and electrons

terms.def: A subatomic particle found in shells around the nucleus with relative mass approximately 0 and relative charge −1.
terms.lessonName: Atomic structure — protons, neutrons and electrons

terms.def: The tiny, dense, positively charged centre of an atom, containing protons and neutrons. It has a radius much smaller than that of the whole atom.
terms.lessonName: Atomic structure — protons, neutrons and electrons

terms.def: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom. It identifies the element and equals the number of electrons in a neutral atom.
terms.lessonName: Atomic structure — protons, neutrons and electrons

terms.def: The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
terms.lessonName: Atomic structure — protons, neutrons and electrons

terms.def: Atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, giving them different mass numbers. They have the same chemical properties.
terms.lessonName: Atomic structure — protons, neutrons and electrons

terms.def: The weighted average mass of all naturally occurring isotopes of an element, compared to 1/12 the mass of a carbon-12 atom. It takes into account the relative abundance of each isotope.
terms.lessonName: Atomic structure — protons, neutrons and electrons

terms.def: Thomson's model of the atom: a ball of positive charge with electrons embedded throughout, like plums in a pudding. Replaced by Rutherford's nuclear model.
terms.lessonName: Atomic structure — protons, neutrons and electrons

terms.def: Rutherford's model: a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at the centre of the atom, surrounded by mostly empty space with electrons orbiting at a distance.
terms.lessonName: Atomic structure — protons, neutrons and electrons

terms.def: Rutherford's experiment in which alpha particles were fired at a thin sheet of gold foil. Most passed straight through, but a small number were deflected at large angles or bounced back, providing evidence for a small, dense, positive nucleus.
terms.lessonName: Atomic structure — protons, neutrons and electrons

terms.def: The scientist who created the first successful periodic table (1869), arranging elements in order of atomic mass and leaving gaps for elements not yet discovered, whose properties he predicted.
terms.lessonName: The periodic table — how it's organised and why

terms.def: A table of all known elements arranged in order of increasing atomic number, so that elements with similar chemical properties appear in the same vertical column (group).
terms.lessonName: The periodic table — how it's organised and why

terms.def: A vertical column in the periodic table. Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outer shell and therefore similar chemical properties.
terms.lessonName: The periodic table — how it's organised and why

terms.def: A horizontal row in the periodic table. The period number equals the number of electron shells the atoms in that period have.
terms.lessonName: The periodic table — how it's organised and why

terms.def: An element with properties intermediate between metals and non-metals — e.g. silicon; used as semiconductors
terms.lessonName: The periodic table — how it's organised and why

terms.def: A material that conducts electricity under some conditions but not others — e.g. silicon in computer chips
terms.lessonName: The periodic table — how it's organised and why

terms.def: The Group 1 elements (lithium, sodium, potassium, etc.). They are highly reactive metals, each with one electron in their outer shell, and react with water to form a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas.
terms.lessonName: The periodic table — how it's organised and why

terms.def: A compound containing a metal ion and OH⁻ ions (e.g. sodium hydroxide, NaOH), formed when an alkali metal reacts with water.
terms.lessonName: The periodic table — how it's organised and why

terms.def: The Group 7 elements (fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine, etc.). They are reactive non-metals that exist as diatomic molecules and form −1 ions by gaining one electron.
terms.lessonName: The periodic table — how it's organised and why

terms.def: A molecule consisting of exactly two atoms bonded together. All halogens exist as diatomic molecules in their elemental form (e.g. Cl₂, F₂, Br₂, I₂).
terms.lessonName: The periodic table — how it's organised and why

terms.def: The Group 0 elements (helium, neon, argon, etc.). They are unreactive because they have a full outer electron shell, so they have no tendency to gain, lose, or share electrons.
terms.lessonName: The periodic table — how it's organised and why

terms.def: A pure substance made up of only one type of atom. It cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means.
A 1- or 2-letter code used to represent an element, with the first letter always capitalised (e.g. Na for sodium, Fe for iron).
A pure substance formed when two or more elements are chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio. Its properties are different from those of the elements it contains.
Suffix indicating a compound made of only two elements (e.g. sodium chloride, magnesium oxide)
Suffix indicating a compound that contains oxygen alongside other elements (e.g. calcium carbonate)
Two or more substances that are not chemically combined. Each substance retains its individual properties, and the composition can vary. Mixtures can be separated by physical methods.
A physical separation technique that uses a filter to separate an insoluble solid (residue) from a liquid (filtrate).
A separation technique that uses differences in boiling point to separate liquids; the liquid is evaporated and the vapour condensed back to liquid in a collecting flask.

A separation technique in which substances in a mixture travel different distances through a stationary phase (e.g. paper) carried by a mobile phase (solvent), separating them based on their different solubilities and attractions to the stationary phase.
The liquid that passes through the filter paper during filtration.
The insoluble solid that remains on the filter paper after filtration.
A separation technique in which a solution is heated to concentrate it and then cooled slowly, causing a pure solid to crystallise out.
A separation technique that uses a fractionating column to separate a mixture of liquids with different boiling points; liquids with lower boiling points distil off first.

A value used in chromatography to identify substances: Rf = distance moved by the substance ÷ distance moved by the solvent. It is always between 0 and 1, and is specific to a substance in a given solvent.
An average that accounts for the different proportions (abundances) of each isotope
The sum of all relative atomic masses in a chemical formula; has no units
The mass of one mole of a substance in g/mol; numerically equal to Mr
An instrument that separates atoms by their mass-to-charge ratio and measures the abundance of each isotope
A chart showing the relative abundance of each isotope plotted against mass number
The ratio of an ion's mass to its electric charge; used to separate ions in a mass spectrometer
An energy level occupied by electrons around the nucleus; shells fill from the inside outwards

terms.lessonName: Electron configuration and the periodic table

terms.def: A negatively charged ion — formed when an atom gains electrons

terms.lessonName: Ionic bonding — how ions form and hold together

One shared pair of electrons between two atoms
Two shared pairs of electrons between two atoms
A small number of atoms joined by covalent bonds, with weak forces between molecules
Weak forces of attraction between molecules (not the covalent bonds within them)
Room temperature and pressure (25°C, 1 atm)
A lattice of millions of atoms all joined by covalent bonds, with no separate molecules
Electrons not held by any one atom, free to move through a structure — enables electrical conductivity

A structure where bonding extends throughout the entire substance (as opposed to individual molecules)

A substance that transfers heat energy readily; metals conduct thermally via delocalised electrons and ion vibrations
Able to be hammered or pressed into shape without breaking (e.g. gold, copper)
Able to be drawn out into a wire without breaking (e.g. copper, aluminium)
A shiny appearance; caused by delocalised electrons on the metal surface reflecting light
A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements, designed to have improved properties
An alloy of iron and carbon (0.1–2%); stronger and harder than pure iron
An alloy of aluminium and copper; lightweight and strong, used in aircraft
Shatters when struck, because shifting layers bring like charges together, which repel and cause fracture
A 3D arrangement where each atom is bonded to 4 others at 109.5° — the geometry of diamond's carbon atoms
A single layer of graphite; extremely strong and an excellent electrical conductor
A carbon molecule in the form of a hollow sphere or tube (e.g. C₆₀ buckminsterfullerene)
Weak intermolecular forces that hold the layers of graphite together
A giant covalent structure; very hard, high melting point, doesn't conduct electricity; found as quartz
A compound made of individual molecules held together by weak intermolecular forces; low melting point
A particle between 1 and 100 nm in size, containing a few hundred to a few thousand atoms
A unit of length equal to 1×10⁻⁹ m (one billionth of a metre)
The ratio of a particle's surface area to its total volume; increases dramatically as particle size decreases
A cylindrical form of carbon (rolled graphene); extremely strong and an excellent electrical conductor
A physical behaviour that only occurs at very small scales (nanometres), causing properties like colour to differ from bulk material
Using nanoparticles to carry drugs to specific cells (e.g. cancer cells), reducing side effects
A substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up; nanoparticle catalysts are highly effective due to enormous surface area
A protective membrane that prevents most large particles from passing from the blood into the brain; nanoparticles can cross it
The idea that if an action has suspected risks that are not yet fully understood, caution should be taken before widespread use

Concentration expressed in mol/dm³ — moles of solute per dm³ of solution

Impurities (including precious metals) that fall to the bottom during copper purification

A substance that causes another to be reduced — it loses electrons and is itself oxidised

terms.def: Calcium hydroxide solution — turns milky/cloudy white in the presence of CO₂
terms.lessonName: Testing for gases — hydrogen, oxygen, CO₂, chlorine

terms.def: Moistened litmus paper used to test for chlorine — turns red then bleaches white
terms.lessonName: Testing for gases — hydrogen, oxygen, CO₂, chlorine

terms.def: The bleaching agent formed when chlorine dissolves in water
terms.lessonName: Testing for gases — hydrogen, oxygen, CO₂, chlorine

terms.def: A test used to identify metal ions by the colour they produce when heated in a Bunsen flame
A wire made of nickel-chromium alloy, used in flame tests because it does not produce its own colour in a flame
A negative ion containing carbon and oxygen; identified by fizzing with dilute acid to produce CO₂
A negative ion identified by adding BaCl₂ solution — gives a white precipitate of BaSO₄ insoluble in dilute acid
Reagent used to test for halide ions; produces white (Cl⁻), cream (Br⁻), or yellow (I⁻) precipitates
Chemical analysis that identifies which substances are present (not how much) — flame tests and ion precipitation tests are examples
The release of gases from the Earth's interior through volcanic activity; responsible for the early atmosphere
terms.lessonName: Earth's atmosphere — where it came from

terms.def: The atmosphere of early Earth, dominated by CO₂ and water vapour, with very little oxygen
terms.lessonName: Earth's atmosphere — where it came from

terms.def: Water vapour cooling to form liquid water; how the oceans formed as Earth cooled
terms.lessonName: Earth's atmosphere — where it came from

terms.def: Calcium carbonate sedimentary rock; formed from marine organisms that used dissolved CO₂ to make shells, locking carbon into rock
terms.lessonName: Earth's atmosphere — where it came from

terms.def: The process by which plants and algae convert CO₂ and H₂O into glucose and O₂ using light energy; responsible for increasing atmospheric O₂
terms.lessonName: Earth's atmosphere — where it came from

terms.def: Ancient sedimentary rock layers containing iron oxide; evidence that early O₂ was absorbed by iron in the oceans before building up in the atmosphere
terms.lessonName: Earth's atmosphere — where it came from

terms.def: The most abundant gas in today's atmosphere (~78%); very unreactive due to strong triple bond, so it accumulated as other gases were removed
terms.lessonName: Earth's atmosphere — where it came from

terms.def: Noble gas making up ~1% of the atmosphere; chemically unreactive, accumulated from radioactive decay in Earth's crust
terms.lessonName: Earth's atmosphere — where it came from

terms.def: The process by which greenhouse gases in the atmosphere absorb infrared radiation from Earth's surface and re-emit it, trapping heat energy and warming the planet
Long-wavelength electromagnetic radiation emitted by warm objects (including Earth's surface) — absorbed by greenhouse gases
Gases that absorb and re-emit infrared radiation: carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄), water vapour, nitrous oxide
A greenhouse gas produced by combustion of fossil fuels, deforestation, and respiration — its atmospheric concentration has increased significantly since industrialisation
A potent greenhouse gas produced by decomposition (landfill, wetlands), livestock digestion, and natural gas leaks
Long-term shifts in global temperatures and weather patterns, primarily driven by increased greenhouse gas concentrations from human activity
Ancient air bubbles trapped in polar ice, used to reconstruct past atmospheric CO₂ concentrations and temperatures over hundreds of thousands of years
A gas produced when fuels containing sulfur impurities are burned — dissolves in rain to form acid rain
Rain with a pH lower than normal (below 5.6) due to dissolved SO₂ and NOₓ — damages ecosystems, buildings, and metals
The removal of sulfur from fossil fuels before they are burned, to reduce SO₂ emissions
Gases formed when atmospheric nitrogen and oxygen react at high temperatures in combustion engines — contribute to acid rain and smog
A type of air pollution formed when NOₓ and unburned hydrocarbons react in sunlight, producing ozone and other irritants
A device fitted to vehicle exhausts that uses a catalyst to convert harmful CO and NOₓ into less harmful CO₂ and N₂
A natural resource that exists in limited quantities and cannot be replenished on a human timescale — e.g. fossil fuels, metal ores
A natural resource that can be replenished naturally within a human lifetime — e.g. timber, solar energy, crops
A finite fossil fuel that is both a source of energy and a feedstock for producing plastics, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, and other materials
Development that meets present needs without preventing future generations from meeting their own needs
The recovery and reprocessing of materials from used products, reducing the need to extract new finite resources
Plastics made from plant-based (renewable) raw materials rather than crude oil
A raw material used to make other chemical products — crude oil is both a fuel and a feedstock for the chemical industry
A fuel made from plant material (biomass); potentially carbon-neutral as the plants absorb CO₂ as they grow
Producing no net addition of CO₂ to the atmosphere — CO₂ released equals CO₂ absorbed
Water that is safe to drink — has low dissolved mineral levels and no harmful microorganisms; not necessarily chemically pure
Water containing only H₂O molecules — no dissolved substances; not the same as potable water
Water that has collected in underground rock layers (aquifers), a source of potable water
The process of allowing particles to settle out of water in large tanks — the first stage of water treatment
Adding controlled amounts of chlorine to water to kill harmful microorganisms — the final stage of water treatment
The process of removing dissolved salts from sea water to produce potable water — by distillation or reverse osmosis
A desalination method that forces sea water through a semi-permeable membrane under high pressure, separating pure water from dissolved salts
A systematic method for evaluating the total environmental impact of a product across all four stages of its life: extraction, manufacture, use, and disposal
The total amount of CO₂ (and equivalent greenhouse gases) produced through all stages of a product's or activity's life cycle
A material that can be broken down by microorganisms into simpler substances — biodegradable waste causes less long-term environmental damage
The order of preference for dealing with waste: reduce → reuse → recycle → recovery → disposal (landfill being last resort)
